items.sentence_raw: In 1942 Allan R Holmberg, a doctoral student in anthropology from Yale University, USA, ventured deep into the jungle of Bolivian Amazonia and searched out an isolated band of Siriono Indians.
items.explain: Q13: Paragraph A describes Holmberg's 1942 trip to study the Siriono — this is *'early research'* among Amazonian Indians. The heading **v** (*'Early research among the Indian Amazons'*) matches perfectly. So the answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: The Siriono, Holmberg later wrote, led a "strikingly backward" existence.
Their villages were little more than clusters of thatched huts.

Life itself was a perpetual and punishing search for food: some families grew manioc and other starchy crops in small garden plots cleared from the forest, while other members of the tribe scoured the country for small game and promising fish holes.
When local resources became depleted, the tribe moved on.
As for technology, Holmberg noted, the Siriono "may be classified among the most handicapped peoples of the world".
items.explain: Q22: Holmberg said the Siriono *'may be classified among the most handicapped peoples of the world'* — **'most handicapped'** means extremely **primitive** in technology. Option **C** (*'were an extremely primitive society'*) matches this. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Other than bows, arrows and crude digging sticks, the only tools the Siriono seemed to possess were "two machetes worn to the size of pocket-knives".
Although the lives of the Siriono have changed in the intervening decades, the image of them as Stone Age relics has endured.
Indeed, in many respects the Siriono epitomize the popular conception of life in Amazonia.

To casual observers, as well as to influential natural scientists and regional planners, the luxuriant forests of Amazonia seem ageless, unconquerable, a habitat totally hostile to human civilization.
The apparent simplicity of Indian ways of life has been judged an evolutionary adaptation to forest ecology, living proof that Amazonia could not - and cannot - sustain a more complex society.
items.explain: Q14: Paragraph B says the simple Indian life was seen as *'living proof that Amazonia could not — and cannot — sustain a more complex society'*. This directly matches heading **i** (*'Amazonia as unable to sustain complex societies'*). So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: Archaeological traces of far more elaborate cultures have been dismissed as the ruins of invaders from outside the region, abandoned to decay in the uncompromising tropical environment.
The popular conception of Amazonia and its native residents would be enormously consequential if it were true.
But the human history of Amazonia in the past 11,000 years betrays that view as myth.
items.explain: Q17: The question says there is a **crucial popular misconception** about Amazonian history. The passage says the popular view is a *'myth'* — **'myth'** means a false belief, which is exactly a **misconception**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Evidence gathered in recent years from anthropology and archaeology indicates that the region has supported a series of indigenous cultures for eleven thousand years; an extensive network of complex societies - some with populations perhaps as large as 100,000 - thrived there for more than 1,000 years before the arrival of Europeans.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says recent evidence shows the region supported *'indigenous cultures for eleven thousand years'* with *'complex societies'*. This means the remains are from **early indigenous communities** — option **A**. ***Option B is a trap*** — the passage says invaders' ruins idea was *'dismissed'*, meaning rejected. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: (Indeed, some contemporary tribes, including the Siriono, still live among the earthworks of earlier cultures.)
Far from being evolutionarily retarded, prehistoric Amazonian people developed technologies and cultures that were advanced for their time.

If the lives of Indians today seem "primitive", the appearance is not the result of some environmental adaptation or ecological barrier; rather it is a comparatively recent adaptation to centuries of economic and political pressure.
items.explain: Q16: The question says prehistoric inhabitants were **backward** in technology. But the passage says their simple life today is *'not the result of some environmental adaptation'* but from recent *'economic and political pressure'* — and earlier it says they had *'advanced'* technologies. So the statement is wrong — answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Investigators who argue otherwise have unwittingly projected the present onto the past.
The evidence for a revised view of Amazonia will take many people by surprise.
Ecologists have assumed that tropical ecosystems were shaped entirely by natural forces and they have focused their research on habitats they believe have escaped human influence.
items.explain:
Q19: The question says most ecologists **were aware** of human shaping. But the passage says ecologists *'assumed that tropical ecosystems were shaped entirely by natural forces'* — **'assumed'** means they believed the opposite, they did **not** know about human influence. So the answer is **NO**.

Q24: The question says the assumption that nature alone shaped Amazonia has been shown **incorrect**. The passage says ecologists *'assumed'* this, but new *'archaeological evidence'* proves it wrong — so option **B** (*'has been shown to be incorrect by recent research'*) is right. ***Option C is a trap*** — Feinsinger said leaving people out is *'no longer tenable'*, meaning the old assumption is wrong, not that he made it. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: But as the University of Florida ecologist, Peter Feinsinger, has noted, an approach that leaves people out of the equation is no longer tenable.
The archaeological evidence shows that the natural history of Amazonia is to a surprising extent tied to the activities of its prehistoric inhabitants.
items.explain:
Q15: Paragraph D states that *'the natural history of Amazonia is to a surprising extent tied to the activities of its prehistoric inhabitants'*. This means prehistoric people **influenced** the natural history — exactly what heading **vi** says. So the answer is **vi**.

The passage says ecologists *'assumed'* this, but new *'archaeological evidence'* proves it wrong — so option **B** (*'has been shown to be incorrect by recent research'*) is right. ***Option C is a trap*** — Feinsinger said leaving people out is *'no longer tenable'*, meaning the old assumption is wrong, not that he made it. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The realization comes none too soon.

In June 1992 political and environmental leaders from across the world met in Rio de Janeiro to discuss how developing countries can advance their economies without destroying their natural resources.
The challenge is especially difficult in Amazonia.
Because the tropical forest has been depicted as ecologically unfit for large-scale human occupation, some environmentalists have opposed development of any kind.
Ironically, one major casualty of that extreme position has been the environment itself.
While policy makers struggle to define and implement appropriate legislation, development of the most destructive kind has continued apace over vast areas.

The other major casualty of the "naturalism" of environmental scientists has been the indigenous Amazonians, whose habits of hunting, fishing, and slash-and-burn cultivation often have been represented as harmful to the habitat.
In the clash between environmentalists and developers, the Indians, whose presence is in fact crucial to the survival of the forest, have suffered the most.
items.explain: Q20: The question says Indians are **necessary** to the forest's well-being. The passage says their presence is *'in fact crucial to the survival of the forest'* — **'crucial'** means **'necessary'**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: The new understanding of the pre-history of Amazonia, however, points toward a middle ground.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says the new understanding *'points toward a middle ground'* and that with good management more people could live there. This would **change policies** — option **C**. ***Option A is a trap*** — the passage says opposing all development was an *'extreme position'* that hurt the environment, so the new view would not warn against all development. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Archaeology makes clear that with judicious management selected parts of the region could support more people than anyone thought before.
items.explain:
Q21: The question says certain parts could support a **higher population**. The passage says *'selected parts of the region could support more people than anyone thought before'* — **'more people'** means a **higher population**. So the answer is **YES**.

This would **change policies** — option **C**. ***Option A is a trap*** — the passage says opposing all development was an *'extreme position'* that hurt the environment, so the new view would not warn against all development. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: The long-buried past, it seems, offers hope for the future.
